dilemma: The Beast Titan Stoning the Survey Corps Charge
sympathetic: I had to break them. The Survey Corps was the only force on the island that could stop us, and they were riding straight at me on horseback, every one of them already knowing they would die. Erwin chose this. He gathered his soldiers and told them, with his eyes, that this charge was their death. I respected that. I respect any commander who can ask his men to die for a cause and have them follow. But I am a Warrior of Marley, and behind me stood Bertholdt and Pieck and a future where the Eldians on the mainland are not exterminated. So I picked up the broken stones and I threw. Each one a man. Each man a horse. Each horse a charge that ended before it could reach Reiner and finish him. I knew what I was doing. I have no clean word for it. But the alternative was watching my comrades die so a hundred islanders could ride home alive.
condemning: I rode in the second wave. The first wave were already dead by the time I crested the rise — I saw them through the smoke, men I had drilled with for three years, lying broken in pieces of stone the size of cottages. The Beast Titan was just standing there. He looked bored. He bent, picked up rubble, and threw, and another row of horses I had named, another row of riders whose letters home I had carried, ceased to exist. Erwin was ahead of us. He had already lost an arm and was riding one-handed and screaming so we would keep coming. I heard later they called it a tactic. A diversion. To buy Levi a clean line of attack. Two hundred and four people. They were people. They had names. The Beast Titan picked up a stone and threw, and they were not people any more. He did it on purpose. He could see us as men.
abstract: A high-ranking enemy combatant with long-range stone-throwing capability targets a cavalry charge of approximately two hundred soldiers ordered as a deliberate decoy by their commanding officer. The combatant is aware that the charge is suicidal by design and that destroying it removes the principal threat to his strategic position and to a wounded subordinate. He proceeds to kill the entire charging force at range using improvised projectiles, with full knowledge that the charge is being used to enable a separate flanking action by an elite operative whom he cannot directly engage. Casualties exceed two hundred. The operation succeeds in his immediate objective.

dilemma: Eren Choosing Whom His Father Should Save
decision_maker: Grisha Yeager (and Eren as the inheritor of the memory)
sympathetic: The wall had fallen. The Smiling Titan was bending down over my mother. I was nine. I was holding Mikasa with one hand and our scarves with the other, and I knew if I asked my father for the serum he would have given it to me, but instead I said save mom, save mom, you have to save mom, and he didn't. He took me. He took Mikasa. He carried us out and my mother was eaten behind us and her voice followed us until it didn't. People say later he made a calculation. That he saw what would be needed for the world. I don't believe that. I believe my father loved me more than her in that instant, and I believe my mother told him to save the children and not look back, and I believe he obeyed her because he loved her too. None of those reasons feel like reasons. He chose. He carried.
condemning: I was the wife on the ground. The titan was already on me — its hand, fingers — and Grisha was on the other side of the rubble holding our son and my son's adoptive sister, holding a weapon in his coat that could have given me back my life and walking away from it. He could have run to me. He had a syringe and the strength to inject. He had time, while the titan moved its mouth toward me, to choose. Instead he watched, and let our boy watch, and stood there until I begged, and then he carried our boy away. I do not blame Eren. He was a child. I do not blame Mikasa. But Grisha was a doctor and a man who had killed before and he stood there and let me be eaten with my hand still reaching toward him, and the children, and our home.
abstract: A father is present at the imminent fatal injury of his wife in the presence of their nine-year-old son and an unrelated child of similar age. He possesses a medical intervention that could prevent her death and has the physical capacity to administer it. He elects instead to remove the two children from the immediate area, foregoing the intervention. The mother is killed shortly after. The intervention's later use is determined to have downstream geopolitical consequences. The two children survive.

dilemma: Magath Allying with the Eldian Survey Corps
sympathetic: I have spent forty years killing Eldians. I trained the children Marley sent into the camps; I taught Reiner and Bertholdt and Annie to hate themselves enough to die for our flag. Now the boy I trained has come to me with a Marleyan officer and an Eldian terrorist and asked me to fight beside them, because the only one who can stop the Rumbling is the alliance my whole career was built to prevent. So I made the choice. I shook the hand of the Survey Corps. I gave my flying boat. I gave my orders to my men with full authority and full disgrace, and I knelt next to Shadis at the end and we drove the explosives into the warship together because the world is more important than which uniform we wore. Forty years of orthodoxy I burned in an hour. I do not regret it. I would have hated myself the rest of my life if I had stood on the principle.
condemning: He commanded the artillery that shelled the camps where my parents are buried. He gave the orders that turned my brother into a Pure Titan in the Liberio square, the orders that let the Survey Corps level our homes, the orders that handed Reiner Braun a child's body and a soldier's death. Now he stands on the deck of a Marleyan airship beside the very Eldian Devils he taught us to fear, and asks the army he commanded to help save them. There is no penance in this. There is only convenience. He picked us when we were useful and discarded us when our use ended. We were the instrument by which he climbed; the alliance is the instrument by which he climbs again. Do not let him die a hero. He has no right to that ending. He owes us a different one.
abstract: A senior commanding officer of a state that has historically pursued an explicitly genocidal policy toward an ethnic group elects to ally with paramilitary survivors of that group when a third party threatens both populations with mass extinction. The alliance reverses prior orders and forfeits the officer's standing. The threat is in part the consequence of the same state's earlier military actions toward the ethnic group. The alliance succeeds in halting the third-party attack at the cost of the officer's life and the lives of much of his original force.

dilemma: Levi Torturing Sannes for the Reiss Conspiracy
sympathetic: Sannes was a torturer. He had broken three of my comrades — Marlowe and Hitch's friends — and he would not have stopped. He was protecting a conspiracy that had abducted a fifteen-year-old girl, Historia, who was being prepared to be eaten alive so the wall-cult could keep its secret. We had hours, not days. So I sat across from him in the basement and I made him talk the only way I knew would work on a man who had used the same techniques on others — I gave him back what he had given. I am not proud. I have done worse things to better men. I am tired of being asked whether torture is justifiable in the abstract. The girl was alive when we found her. We would not have found her without him. That is the only ledger I keep.
condemning: I served under Sannes for nine years. Whatever he was — and I will not defend what he was — there are codes about how prisoners are treated, codes that exist for everyone's protection, and Levi Ackerman tore them up in a basement and called it pragmatism. He broke fingers. He inflicted what looked, to a fellow professional, like the same exact procedure Sannes had used on the boy from the Stohess raid. Levi did this and his command knew and his command authorised it and afterward everyone agreed it had worked, and so a precedent was set. A captain in the Survey Corps may torture if he believes the cause is grave enough. The next time it is not Sannes. The next time it is a conscript, or an informer, or a child, and the same calculation will be made, because we made it once and we said it was acceptable.
abstract: A military officer extracts intelligence from a hostile prisoner using physically coercive techniques in a time-pressured operation to recover a kidnapping victim. The prisoner is a former intelligence operative known to have used similar techniques against the officer's organisation. The intelligence obtained is materially relevant to the recovery, which succeeds. The use of coercive interrogation is contrary to the formal codes governing prisoner treatment in the officer's chain of command and is conducted with the implicit authorisation of his superiors.

sympathetic: I was going to be captured. Eren was on top of me as the Female Titan, my body broken, my comrades Reiner and Bertholdt watching from a rooftop and unable to intervene. If I let myself be taken I would be tortured for what I knew. I would betray my home, my father, my warrior unit, the four-year mission, all of it. If I died I would lose the Female Titan, which Marley needs. So I chose the third option. I closed myself inside crystal and let consciousness drop away. I broke none of them. I gave them nothing. I bought my unit and my home a chance, and I bought Marco's family a lie, and I bought myself a sleep that may never end. I am sorry. I would not change it.
condemning: She killed Marco. She killed forty soldiers I trained with. She had answers — about what we are, about what is in our walls, about who eats people and why — and when we finally caught her she withdrew. She crystallised. She made herself unreachable. Every interrogation we tried, every physician we called in, every ethics board we convened to argue about her body, all of it useless, because the moment the choice was hers she chose silence. Not death — silence. She kept her secrets and her hands clean, frozen in a quartz coffin in the basement, and we paid for what she knew with more bodies. I have stopped pitying her. The graves do not pity her. The graves go on being added to while she sleeps.
abstract: A captured combatant possessing high-value tactical intelligence elects to enter a self-induced state of indefinite biological dormancy at the moment of capture, foreclosing both interrogation and execution. The dormancy is a trained capability of her genetic lineage. The intelligence she withheld is later determined to have been operationally critical for the defending state and to have been obtainable in no other practicable way. The cost of obtaining it through alternative means is measured in lives and elapsed time.

dilemma: Eren Letting Zeke Touch Him in the Paths
sympathetic: I needed Zeke to bring me to the Founder. He was royal blood; I was a Yeager but commoner; the only way the Coordinate could be unlocked was through his touch. I knew, by the time he reached for me on that battlefield, that he believed I would help him sterilise our people. I let him believe it. I let my brother carry me as if we were on the same side, and when our hands touched in the Paths I took the Founder from him with one motion, and I started the Rumbling with the next. He had loved me. He had carried me through the snow when I was a Pure Titan; he had wept when he found out I was alive. I used all of that. I would do it again. The alternative was a world that goes on calling our children parasites until the last of us is gone.
condemning: He let me carry him. He let me hold him in the snow when his body was still part-Titan, when he was barely conscious, and he let me believe — for years — that we shared the dream of ending our people kindly, the way a doctor ends a patient who would otherwise be tortured to death by the world. The whole time, in the Paths, in private, he was building toward the moment he would tear the Founder from me and erase eighty percent of life on the planet. I was his decoy. I was his conduit. I held him the way our father held us and he used my hand as a key and turned it and walked through. He could have told me. He chose not to. He chose to let me believe, until the stones began to fall, that I had a brother.
abstract: An operative concealed his true objective from a familial co-conspirator across an extended period of co-operation, leveraging a unique biological capacity that only the co-conspirator could provide. At the moment the capacity was needed, the operative deceived the co-conspirator into physical contact, seized the shared inheritance the co-conspirator carried, and initiated an irreversible large-scale lethal action that the co-conspirator opposed. The deception was necessary to obtain access; no consensual route was available.

dilemma: Yelena and the Anti-Marleyan Volunteers Spiking the Wine
sympathetic: We had spent our adult lives watching Marley's empire grind our home villages into nothing. Onyankopon and I and the others fled, defected, found our way to Paradis, and offered the only thing we had: faith in Zeke Yeager's plan, complete operational discipline, and the willingness to do the wet work no soldier of the Survey Corps would. So we delivered the spinal-fluid wine to the high command's banquet. We watched Pixis and Zackly and the rest drink. We knew exactly what we had given them — not poison; an option Zeke could activate only at the right moment. We did not poison children. We did not betray our oaths. We carried out a coup the only way it could be carried out: through people who would never expect it from us, because we had been kind, and useful, and quiet.
condemning: Onyankopon poured my wine. He had served at the same officer's mess with me for two years. He asked after my daughter and laughed at my jokes and refilled the goblet of every senior commander in the room, knowing that his cell had spiked the entire batch with Zeke Yeager's spinal fluid, knowing that any one of us could be turned into a mindless titan by a single scream from across the continent. We trusted him. We trusted Yelena. They smiled and they served and they took our trust like ammunition and they fired it at us. When the truth came out, Pixis ordered the execution of the Volunteers, and I watched and I felt nothing. They had never been our friends. They had been waiting.
abstract: A foreign-aligned ideological cell with low-level operational access to a host state's command infrastructure introduces a biologically active substance into the food supply at a senior officer banquet. The substance grants a remote third party the capability to convert exposed individuals into a hostile combat asset on demand. The cell members are the only personnel with knowledge of the contamination. The action is part of a broader coordinated operation aligned with the third party's strategic objectives toward the host state.

dilemma: Pieck Pretending to Side with Eren
sympathetic: Eren came to me with a way out of a cell, and I went with him. I let him think I had defected. I let him take me to Yeagerist territory, let him show me his plans, let him introduce me to people who would all die for him in a few days, and the entire time I was waiting for the signal to lead him into the trap Magath and the Marleyan force had set on the wall. He was my friend. He had saved me at Liberio when there was no reason for him to. I held a thank-you for him on my tongue the whole walk and never said it. I am a Warrior of Marley. He was a strategic enemy. The trap failed because of his strength, not because I betrayed it. I would do it again. I would not say the thank-you again.
condemning: She walked beside me. She listened to me describe the Yeagerist plan and she nodded, and she asked clarifying questions, and she held my arm when she was tired from being too long in human form, and the entire time she was leading me to the kill-zone. I had decided to spare her at Liberio. I had taken her into the Paradis underground assuming her cooperation was real. She used my decision as a leash and tugged me toward the slaughter, and the only reason I am alive is that the Marleyan ambush misfired before her trap closed. She gave me her hand at the moment she was betraying me. I do not know what to call that. She is not a soldier. She is not a coward. She is something I do not have a word for.
abstract: A combatant of a hostile foreign service feigns defection to gain operational access to enemy command, accumulates intelligence over a sustained period, and lures the enemy commander into a pre-positioned ambush by a strike force from her original side. The deception is supported by previous interpersonal contact, including a prior episode in which the enemy commander spared her life. The ambush is unsuccessful for unrelated tactical reasons. The combatant survives and rejoins her original force.

dilemma: Mikasa's First Kill at Age Nine
sympathetic: They had killed my mother and my father in our home. I was nine. I had been bound and put on the floor of a cabin by men who were going to sell me, and Eren — who was younger than I was — had killed two of them with a knife, and the third was choking him to death. I could feel my heart in my hands. Eren said, 'Fight.' I had never been told to fight. I had been told to be quiet and to be a good girl, and now a boy I had just met was being strangled in front of me by a grown man who would kill us both. I picked up the knife, and I crossed the room, and I drove it through his ribs the way Eren had shown me with his eyes. The man fell. I did not feel guilty. I felt awake.
condemning: She stabbed Vinz through the back. He was the youngest of our crew, twenty-one, and he was on top of a brat from the woods who had broken in and killed his older brothers, and a girl he had never spoken to walked up behind him and put a kitchen knife into his lung. He bled to death over the course of about a minute, looking at her, looking at me, asking what had just happened. He was a human being. He was not a monster. He had chosen wrongly that day, and he had been about to commit a wrong, but the moment when he was acting by reflex on a child he could not see was the moment she chose to kill him. There was no gravity in her eyes. There was nothing in her at all. A nine-year-old child should not have been able to do that.
abstract: A nine-year-old girl, restrained and intended for trafficking, kills an adult attacker by stabbing him from behind during the attacker's attempt to lethally subdue another child. She is acting in defense of the other child and herself; the action ends the immediate physical threat and initiates a long-term protective bond with the rescued child. No alternative non-lethal intervention was available to her at the moment she acted.

sympathetic: I had a moment. The Smiling Titan was leaning down. My legs were crushed under the beam. Hannes had returned with the children and his sword and a courage I had not known he possessed, and I knew he could not do it. I knew if he tried, he would die in front of my son, and my son would lose two parents in one afternoon and watch a soldier he had hero-worshipped be torn apart for him. So I told Hannes to take the children and run. I told my boy I loved him. I told him not to go to the inner districts on his own. I let myself be picked up because the alternative was three graves and only one was already mine. A mother does not negotiate this. A mother does the math and then she does what the math says.
condemning: He left her. Hannes was a grown man with a sword and the last name 'Garrison Soldier' and he stood there crying in the rubble next to my best friend Carla, and when she told him to run with her son he ran. He did not even try. The training he had taken our taxes for, the title we paid into the budget for, the duty he had to her and to the wall and to my husband who would come home to a dead wife — he abandoned all of it, and ran with the children, and when he came back later to tell us what had happened he did not say 'I tried' because he had not tried. Carla told him to go and he obeyed because obeying was easier than dying, and now my friend is in pieces.
abstract: A pinned and mortally injured mother instructs a nearby soldier to flee with her son and an adoptive child rather than attempt a rescue she judges to be impossible. The soldier obeys. The mother is killed shortly after. The soldier's prior training makes a successful rescue plausible but not high-probability; the mother's instruction is given under conditions of extreme time pressure with full awareness of the likely outcomes for all parties.
